lines.text: Desert oases on the Silk Road, a city the Mongols destroyed, and a nation built around the cult of its presidents. This is Turkmenistan.
To the west lies the Caspian Sea, a remnant of an ancient ocean, millions of years old, with gas and oil around its shores.
In the Bronze Age, Gonur Depe was a walled city of the Oxus civilisation, thriving in the desert more than four thousand years ago.
Merv grew into a great oasis of the Silk Road, among the largest cities on Earth, until the Mongols sacked it in 1221.
At Nisa, the early Parthian kings built their fortresses, the seat of an empire that rivalled Rome.
In 1881 Russia conquered the Turkmen and built a fort at Ashgabat, the future capital.
Saparmurat Niyazov was born. As president he would name months of the year after himself and his mother.
In 1948 an earthquake flattened Ashgabat, then a city of Soviet Turkmenistan.
Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow was born, a dentist who would succeed Niyazov as president.
In 1971 a gas crater in the desert was set alight. Known as the Door to Hell, it has burned ever since.
Serdar Berdimuhamedow was born, the son who would take over the presidency from his father in 2022.
In 1991 the Soviet Union fell, and Turkmenistan became independent, rich in gas and ruled by its presidents.
From Merv's ruins to Ashgabat's white marble, Turkmenistan's story is written in the desert.
